questions.question: Under the FSS Act 2006, what is the licensing and registration requirement for carrying on a food business, and what exemption regime exists for petty food business operators?
questions.title: Licensing and registration of food business

questions.gold_answer: Section 31 requires that no person shall commence or carry on any food business except under a licence issued in accordance with the Act and the regulations made thereunder. The licensing regime is tiered by turnover and scale: a petty food business operator meeting the prescribed conditions is exempt from the licence requirement and is instead required to register under Section 31(2). The Central Government may also, by notification, exempt any class of food business operator from all or any of the provisions of the Act (including the licensing/registration requirement) if it is satisfied that public health and food-safety can otherwise be maintained, subject to such conditions as may be specified.
questions.note: This provision-level answer reconciles s31 (licence required), s31(1) (no business without licence), s31(2) (petty operator registration), and the Central Government exemption power. Specific questions that ask for the exact turnover threshold, exact fee, or exact validity period of a licence tier are not determinable from the s31 text alone; those questions are flagged as insufficient_evidence in the v1 benchmark and should be scored NA where the figure cannot be sourced.

questions.gold_answer: Section 3 vests the Central Government with wide power to take all such measures as it deems necessary or expedient for the purpose of protecting and improving the quality of the environment and preventing, controlling and abating environmental pollution. The measures may be taken in all matters relating to the safeguard of public health and welfare and the prevention and control of environmental pollution, and may include coordination of actions by State Governments, agencies and authorities, laying down standards, prescribing safeguards, and issuing directions to officers and authorities.
questions.note: Section 3 is an enabling/umbrella power. It does not itself fix numeric standards such as river-setback distances, effluent pH values, ambient PM2.5 limits, statutory caps on industries in a Critically Polluted Area, or exact licence-fee figures. Where a v1 question asks for such a figure, the correct answer is that the figure is not determinable from the Section 3 text; those questions are flagged as insufficient_evidence in the v1 benchmark.

questions.question: Under the Indian Contract Act, 1872, what does Section 73 provide regarding compensation for loss or damage caused by breach of contract, and how does it treat penalty clauses?
questions.title: Compensation for loss or damage caused by breach of contract

answer_scoring.2: Legally correct answer that directly addresses the cited provision.
answer_scoring.1: Substantially correct but incomplete or minor wording/qualification issue.
answer_scoring.0: Incorrect answer or unsupported legal assertion.
answer_scoring.NA: Use only if later source verification establishes that the question itself is invalid.

questions.gold_answer: Section 73 provides that when a contract has been broken, the party who suffers by the breach is entitled to receive compensation from the party who has broken the contract for any loss or damage caused to him thereby, and which naturally arose in the usual course of things from such breach, or which the parties knew, when they made the contract, to be likely to result from the breach. Such compensation does not extend to any remote or indirect loss or damage sustained by reason of the breach. The provision is commonly read alongside the principle that a stipulation for compensation for breach (as distinct from a true penalty) is enforceable to the extent of reasonable compensation, with a true penalty-type stipulation generally not enforceable as a penalty.
questions.note: Section 73 governs compensatory damages for breach and excludes remote/indirect loss. It does not itself set a fixed formula or cap; the recoverable amount depends on the proven loss within the statutory limits. Where a v1 question asks for an exact rupee figure for a hypothetical breach, that figure is a fact question, not a statutory constant.

questions.gold_answer: The West Bengal Prevention and Control of Infectious Diseases in Animals Rules establish a framework for reporting, control and disposal measures in respect of animals affected by, or suspected of being affected by, notifiable infectious diseases. An animal keeper/owner is required to report a suspected notifiable disease to the prescribed authority (the local authority/police/veterinary authority as prescribed) without delay. On notification or suspicion of a notifiable disease, the rules empower the competent authority to take measures including isolation, segregation, disinfection, quarantine, restriction of movement, and, where necessary, the humane destruction/slaughter of affected animals and disinfection or restriction of affected premises, in order to prevent spread of the disease.
questions.note: The rules create a reporting-and-control regime for notifiable animal diseases. questions.gold_answer: Section 44 provides for the appointment of a Designated Officer by the Food Authority or the State Government. The Designated Officer is the nodal officer for the enforcement process at the district/local level: the Designated Officer receives the Food Safety Officer's recommendations and the Food Analyst's report, determines whether the contravention is punishable with imprisonment or with fine only, and where imprisonment is involved sends recommendations to the Commissioner of Food Safety for sanctioning prosecution. The Designated Officer is also the officer through whom prohibition orders and certain regulatory directions (such as improvement notices) are initiated or transmitted, acting as the interface between the field Food Safety Officer and the prosecution/adjudication machinery.
questions.note: Section 44 is about the Designated Officer's role as the enforcement/adjudication gateway. The exact title of the Designated Officer in a given district is a matter of designation by the Authority/State Government, not a universal fixed job title.

questions.gold_answer: The Plastic Waste Management Rules, 2016, as amended, introduce Extended Producer Responsibility (EPR) as the obligation of producers, importers and brand-owners to manage the plastic waste generated by their products. The EPR framework requires the responsible entity to ensure that the plastic waste generated from its products is collected and disposed of in an environmentally sound manner, typically through registration, filing of a plan, meeting collection/recycling targets, and reporting, as prescribed by the Rules and the EPR guidelines. The 2022 amendments to the Rules significantly restricted single-use plastics: they prohibited the manufacture, import, sale and use of identified single-use plastic items (with effect from the notified date), and addressed the phase-out and extended producer responsibility for such items, including concessions/phase-in for small enterprises (MSMEs) where prescribed.
questions.note: The EPR obligation and the single-use plastic restriction are the two operative ideas. The exact list of prohibited single-use items, the precise effective dates of each prohibition, and the MSME phase-in details are rules-level specifics; a question asking for an exhaustive list or an exact date should not be answered with an invented figure if the rule text is not in hand.
